name: Diego Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Valley Hearth Care, which is a small agency run by a married couple, Ray and Linda, out of an office above the hardware shop. Most of my clients are old farmers and their wives up the valley, people who'd rather die than ask for help, so the first job is getting them to let you in. I start at seven with Mr Brandt, who's ninety-one and still tells me how to fix my van. I like that they're proud people, I understand that. What wears me out is the farm tracks in winter, and some of the older men who are heavy to lift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Marta, and we're getting married next August at St Joseph's, where we both grew up. We're renting a small cottage off the main road until we can afford something. Money's tight, I've got maybe two weeks' wages put by, and the wedding's eating whatever's left. I don't use any of that AI stuff, I've got a basic phone and Linda rings me with changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Most of that stuff is hot air anyway, if you ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. People round here don't trust gadgets, and they don't need them to look after their own. I'd say it at church coffee after Mass, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it just means I keep worrying about the same things. The wedding's costing more than we planned, the van needs tyres, and Ray and Linda are getting on, so they might sell the agency one day. If a big chain bought it, I don't know if they'd keep me on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take every extra shift Linda offers before the wedding, and we'd cut the guest list from a hundred and twenty to eighty. I'd ask Ray straight out whether he's planning to sell, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A bit of worry about money, but that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cutting forty guests: how would that go down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly with my mum. She wants every cousin from both sides. But I'd rather start married life without a loan than have every cousin at the wedding. Marta agrees. We'd do a big barbecue afterwards for the ones who didn't make the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Asking Ray if he's selling: is that a hard conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, Ray's straight with people. He'd tell me over a cup of tea. I just haven't asked because I'm scared of the answer.

say: I'd say **I told you so**: people here don't trust gadgets.
I'd say at church coffee that families **look after their own**.
think: I worry about the **wedding costs** and the van's tyres.
The owners might **sell the agency** to a chain one day.
do: Take every **extra shift** Linda offers before the wedding.
Cut the **guest list** from a hundred and twenty to eighty.
Ask Ray directly if he plans to **sell the agency**.
S0.quote: I'd rather start married life without a loan than have every cousin at the wedding.
fieldNote: His pressures are **wedding costs** and a possible agency sale, not AI.
He avoids asking about the sale because he's **scared of the answer**.
His traditional outlook shows in trusting **family and church** over gadgets.

steps.text: Take every extra shift Linda offers before the August wedding
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80
Keep his valley rounds and ask Ray about selling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So computers do the office stuff. Linda does that with a diary and a phone. I can't see her changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people up the valley won't let a computer anywhere near them, and good for them. Care is about trust, and you can't buy trust from a tech company. I'd say businesses should be free to use it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm all right for now. Robots for lifting heavy old farmers are a long way off, and the thinking stuff is Linda's job, not mine. If Ray sells to a chain, though, they'd bring in their computer rota and I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd learn the minimum if a new owner made me use an app. And I'd keep putting money aside for the wedding and the deposit on a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, with a small knot about the agency changing hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever look at another agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's only one other in the valley, and they're a chain already. I'd rather stay with Ray as long as he's there. Loyalty counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marta say if you came home with an app you had to use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh and set it up for me. She's a teaching assistant at the primary school and uses all that. I'd let her, and then I'd grumble about it.

say: I'd say valley people won't let a **computer near them**.
I'd say care is **about trust** and businesses should be free to choose.
think: I think robots for **lifting heavy farmers** are a long way off.
A **chain buyer** would bring in a computer rota I'd hate.
do: Carry on with **valley rounds** as normal.
Learn the **minimum app use** if a new owner insists.
Keep saving for the **wedding** and a **house deposit**.
feel: **Fine**, with a small knot about the **agency changing hands**.
S1.quote: Care is about trust, and you can't buy trust from a tech company.
fieldNote: He sees his **hands-on job** as safe while robots spread slowly.
His real fear is a **chain takeover**, which brings the technology to him.
He values **loyalty** to a local employer over changing jobs.

steps.text: Carry on his valley rounds for Valley Hearth Care
Keep saving for the wedding and a house deposit
Wait to learn any app until a new owner requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028? I don't believe that. And robots lifting people by 2031? No.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's rubbish, and people should stop scaring old folk with it. If it did happen, I'd say families should step up and look after their own, like they used to. I wouldn't want the government paying everyone to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if it was true, I'd be finished in this job by 2031. I've got no other trade and two weeks of savings, and we'd be just married. My dad's got a small building firm, so maybe he'd take me on labouring, but robots would be after that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do nothing for a while, because I wouldn't believe it until the robots were in someone's house. Then I'd ask Dad about labouring for him. And Marta and I would move in with her parents to save the rent, rather than take any handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor dropping out, just when we're starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put the wedding off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd get married at St Joseph's whatever happens. We'd just do it smaller, maybe thirty people and sandwiches in the church hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no handouts. What if there was nothing else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take what I had to and hate it. I'd rather work for less than be paid to do nothing. But I've never been tested on that, so I can't swear to it.

say: I'd say it's **rubbish** meant to scare old folk.
I'd say **families should step up** rather than government paying people.
think: Privately I'd be **finished in care** by 2031.
I've **no other trade** and two weeks' savings, just married.
do: Do nothing until robots **are in homes**.
Ask Dad about **labouring** for his building firm.
Move in with **Marta's parents** to save rent.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor dropping out as they start married life.
S2.quote: I'd rather work for less than be paid to do nothing.
fieldNote: He **rejects the scenario** publicly but privately expects to lose his job.
His plan B is **family**: his father's firm and his in-laws' house.
He admits his **no-handouts** stance hasn't been tested.

steps.text: Wait until robots reach clients' homes before acting
Ask his dad for labouring work at the building firm
Move in with Marta's parents to save rent
Hold a smaller wedding with thirty guests at the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd still not believe it, but I'd have to listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said, that families need to look after their own. I'd say it's up to people to sort themselves out, not wait for the government. I'd probably not talk about it much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough time to get married, maybe start a family, and then the robots come for the work in 2034. That frightens me more than the two-year one, in a way, because there'd be more to lose by then. I'd be thirty-five with kids, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course on the building side, maybe plastering, because Dad's always short of plasterers. I'd keep the care job until it went. And we'd put off trying for a baby by a couple of years until we knew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but I'd lie awake some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off a baby: how would Marta feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Upset. She's wanted children since forever. It'd be a hard talk, probably with her mum in the middle. But I'd rather wait for a baby than not be able to feed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Plastering: wouldn't robots come for that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, around the same time. But Dad says people round here would still rather pay a man they know. Maybe that's me being stubborn.

say: I'd say families must **look after their own**.
I'd say it's up to people to **sort themselves out**, not wait for government.
think: I think robots in 2034 would hit when I've **more to lose**.
I could be **thirty-five with kids** by then.
do: Start an evening **plastering course** for Dad's firm.
Keep the **care job** until it goes.
Put off **trying for a baby** by a couple of years.
S3.quote: I'd rather wait for a baby than not be able to feed one.
fieldNote: He fears a later robot date because he'd have **more to lose** by then.
He'd learn a **trade from family**, not technology.
Delaying children shows **real cost** to his traditional plans.

steps.text: Start an evening plastering course for his dad's firm
Delay trying for a baby by a couple of years
Keep his care rounds at Valley Hearth until they go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be nearly forty when robots come. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no point worrying yet. Plenty can change in ten years, and people adapt. Work hard, look after your family, and you'll be all right, that's what my grandad said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd mostly forget about it for a while. The job's mine for years. If anything, I'd start thinking about it around the time we had a second kid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing different. I'd keep working for Ray, get married, save for a house. Maybe later I'd do the plastering course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. Money's still the worry, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd forget about it. Is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Marta would remind me. She's the planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, and learn to talk to people. Machines can't do both, or that's what I'd hope.

say: I'd say there's **no point worrying** yet, because people adapt.
I'd quote my grandad: **work hard**, look after your family.
think: I think I'd **forget about it** for a while.
I'd start thinking about it around a **second child**.
do: Keep working for Ray and **get married** as planned.
feel: **Calm enough**, with money still the main worry.
S4.quote: Learn a trade, and learn to talk to people. Machines can't do both, or that's what I'd hope.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **put it off**, which he admits is risky.
His fiancée Marta is the **planner** in the household.
His advice for children is **trade plus people skills**.

steps.text: Keep working for Ray at Valley Hearth Care
Save each month towards a house deposit
Get married at St Joseph's next August as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is no time at all, and we'd be just married with nothing saved. What would help is apprenticeships for people like me, paid while you learn, so you can move into a trade without losing your wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old farmers. A lot of my clients would rather go without help than have a robot in the house. Somebody should ask them what they want.

headlineQuote: A lot of my clients would rather go without help than have a robot in the house.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old carer** for a small family-run agency serving old farming families.
He's engaged to Marta, with a **wedding next August** and about two weeks' savings.
He avoids technology and **disbelieves fast change**, waiting for proof before acting.
His fallbacks are **family**: his father's building firm and his in-laws' home.
He is **traditional**, preferring work, family and church to government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, newly married with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** to move into a trade without losing wages.
